questions.stem: Which statement defines an alloy correctly?

options.text: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually metals or carbon
options.explanation: The mixture idea with metallic or carbon partners is the definition of record.

options.text: A pure metal refined until no impurities remain
options.explanation: That is the opposite of an alloy: alloying adds other elements on purpose.

options.text: A compound of a metal with oxygen
options.explanation: A compound is chemically bonded in a fixed ratio; an alloy is a mixture, and oxygen is not the usual partner.

options.text: Any metal extracted from an ore
options.explanation: Extraction produces the metal; alloying is a later, separate step of mixing.

questions.stem: Steel is an alloy of which two substances?

options.text: Iron and carbon
options.explanation: The note gives steel as the example of a metal mixed with the non-metal carbon.

options.text: Copper and zinc
options.explanation: That pair makes brass, the other named alloy.

options.text: Iron and nickel only
options.explanation: Nickel appears in stainless steel, but steel in general is iron with carbon.

options.text: Iron and oxygen
options.explanation: Iron and oxygen make an oxide, which is a compound, not the steel mixture.

questions.stem: What is the composition of brass?

options.text: 70% copper and 30% zinc
options.explanation: These are the exact figures the note quotes for brass.

options.text: 70% zinc and 30% copper
options.explanation: The shares are swapped; copper is the larger part of brass.

options.text: 70% iron and 30% carbon
options.explanation: That would be a very high-carbon steel, not brass.

options.text: 20% chromium and 10% nickel
options.explanation: Those are the stainless steel additions, not brass.

questions.stem: Why are alloys often more useful than pure metals?

options.text: Their enhanced properties, such as being stronger, harder and more corrosion-resistant, fit demanding jobs
options.explanation: The mixture's properties can be very different from the ingredients, which is exactly what makes alloys useful.

options.text: They are always cheaper to extract from ores
options.explanation: Extraction applies to the metal, not the alloy; usefulness comes from the enhanced properties.

options.text: They are lighter than every pure metal
options.explanation: Weight is not the general claim; strength, hardness and resistance are.

options.text: They conduct electricity better than pure metals
options.explanation: Conductivity is not the listed enhancement; alloying usually harms conduction.

questions.stem: Which pairing of alloy and ingredient set is correct?

options.text: Steel with iron and carbon; brass with copper and zinc
options.explanation: Both named alloys match their ingredients exactly as the note lists them.

options.text: Steel with copper and zinc; brass with iron and carbon
options.explanation: Both pairings are swapped between the two alloys.

options.text: Steel with copper and carbon; brass with iron and zinc
options.explanation: Neither pairing matches the note's compositions.

options.text: Steel with iron and zinc; brass with copper and carbon
options.explanation: The partners are crossed over incorrectly in both cases.

questions.stem: Define an alloy in terms of the substances it combines.
questions.modelAnswer: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements — usually other metals, or a non-metal such as carbon.

questions.stem: State the two metals present in brass and the percentage of each.
Explain why alloys, rather than the pure metals they contain, are so often chosen for everyday objects.
questions.modelAnswer: The blend often behaves differently from its ingredients: alloys can be stronger and harder than the pure metals, and many resist corrosion or withstand extreme temperatures, so they last longer in use.

questions.stem: A bicycle maker wants a frame metal that shrugs off wet winters without rusting. Decide whether a pure metal or an alloy fits the need better, naming the property behind your decision.
questions.modelAnswer: An alloy fits: many alloys resist corrosion, so a steel frame (iron mixed with carbon) withstands wet weather far better than a pure metal would.

questions.stem: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?

options.text: Different-sized atoms distort the layers, making them difficult to slide
options.explanation: The distorted, jammed layers are exactly why the alloy resists deformation and so feels harder.

options.text: Alloy atoms are larger, so the metal is more dense
options.explanation: Density is not the mechanism; the sliding of layers is.

options.text: Alloying forms strong new chemical bonds between metals
options.explanation: An alloy is a mixture, so no new compound or bond type is required for the hardness.

options.text: Alloys contain fewer free electrons, so they are stiffer
options.explanation: Electron count governs conduction, not hardness; the layer-sliding story is the answer.

questions.stem: A question shows four particle diagrams. Which one represents an alloy?

options.text: Unevenly sized particles arranged in distorted rows
options.explanation: Mixed sizes and bent rows are the visual signature of the distorted alloy lattice.

options.text: Identical particles in perfectly straight rows
options.explanation: That is the pure metal, whose regular layers slide easily.

options.text: Identical particles in a jumbled gas-like spread
options.explanation: Alloys are solid lattices with distortion, not random spreads.

options.text: Paired particles joined by visible bonds
options.explanation: Molecules with bonds describe compounds, not the mixture structure of an alloy.

questions.stem: Why are pure metals relatively soft?

options.text: Their identical atoms form regular layers that slide over each other easily
options.explanation: Smooth, regular planes slip under force, which is why pure metals deform readily.

options.text: Their atoms are too small to touch
options.explanation: Atoms in a metal are closely packed; softness comes from layer sliding.

options.text: They contain no electrons
options.explanation: Metals are full of delocalised electrons; this has nothing to do with softness.

options.text: Their layers are distorted by impurities
options.explanation: Distortion is the alloy story; pure metals have the undistorted layers.
options.misconception: alloy story applied to pure metals

questions.stem: What effect does adding atoms of a different size have on the metal's structure?

options.text: It distorts the regular arrangement of the atoms
options.explanation: The foreign sizes push the neat rows out of line, which blocks easy sliding.

options.text: It makes the arrangement even more regular
options.explanation: Extra sizes do the opposite: they spoil the regularity.

options.text: It turns the metal into a compound
options.explanation: Mixing does not create a compound; the lattice simply becomes distorted.

options.text: It has no effect until the metal melts
options.explanation: The distortion exists in the solid and is present at everyday temperatures.

questions.stem: Brass is harder than pure copper. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Zinc atoms of a different size distort copper's layers, so they cannot slide easily
options.explanation: Applying the general mechanism to brass: the zinc atoms jam the copper lattice's slip planes.

options.text: Zinc donates extra electrons that stiffen the copper
options.explanation: Electron donation is not the mechanism; distorted layers are.

options.text: Brass is a compound of copper and zinc with new bonds
options.explanation: Brass is a mixture; hardness comes from lattice distortion, not new bonding.

options.text: Copper's layers slide more easily when zinc is present
options.explanation: That would make brass softer, which contradicts the observation.

questions.stem: What does adding atoms of a different size do to the regular arrangement of atoms in a pure metal?
questions.modelAnswer: It distorts the regular rows: the differently sized atoms spoil the neat arrangement of the pure metal lattice.

questions.stem: How does the ease of layer sliding compare between an alloy and its pure metal?
questions.modelAnswer: In the alloy the layers slide far less easily, and that difficulty is exactly why the alloy is harder than the pure metal.

questions.stem: Explain, step by step, why the different atom sizes in an alloy make the metal harder.
questions.modelAnswer: Atoms of different sizes distort the regular rows of the lattice, so the layers can no longer slide smoothly over one another; with slipping made difficult, the alloy resists shaping forces and is harder than the pure metal.

questions.stem: An exam question offers four particle diagrams: A shows neat rows of equal circles, B shows uneven circles sitting in distorted rows, C shows molecules in pairs, D shows a fixed alternating grid. Which diagram represents an alloy, and what feature gave it away?
questions.modelAnswer: Diagram B: uneven-sized particles in distorted rows are the signature of an alloy — the different-sized atoms have spoiled the regular lattice seen in the others.
